content_voiceover: This slide expands the previous overview into a full mechanistic diagram of endothelial antithrombotic activity. On the antiplatelet side, CD39 converts ATP and ADP into AMP, which 5 prime nucleotidase further converts into adenosine, while prostacyclin and nitric oxide directly inhibit platelet aggregation; together these pathways counteract von Willebrand factor's prothrombotic drive. On the anticoagulant side, thrombin bound to thrombomodulin, assisted by EPCR, activates protein C into aPC, which together with protein S degrades factors Va and VIIIa; separately, heparan sulfate potentiates antithrombin to inhibit thrombin, factor Xa, factor IXa, and factor XIa, and TFPI blocks the tissue factor VIIa Xa complex. On the fibrinolytic side, tissue plasminogen activator is balanced against PAI-1 to control the transition from thrombin generation to fibrinolysis. The overall message is that the endothelium is not a passive lining but an active, multi-pathway regulator that keeps coagulation and platelet activation confined and reversible.
keypoints: CD39 and 5'-nucleotidase convert ATP/ADP to antiplatelet adenosine
Thrombomodulin-EPCR-protein C axis inactivates Va and VIIIa
Heparan sulfate-antithrombin axis inhibits thrombin, Xa, IXa, XIa
TFPI blocks tissue factor-VIIa-Xa; t-PA/PAI-1 balance fibrinolysis
keypoint_voiceover: This integrated diagram links three arms: the CD39-adenosine pathway suppresses platelets, the thrombomodulin-EPCR-protein C axis inactivates factors Va and VIIIa, and heparan sulfate boosted antithrombin blocks thrombin, Xa, IXa, and XIa, while TFPI and the t-PA PAI-1 balance round out anticoagulant and fibrinolytic control.
